articles.body: Defending Webhooks: Preventing Signature Forgery, Replay Attacks, and Timing Attacks in Python Background & Threat Model: Why Verification Is Non-Negotiable When integrating third-party webhook receivers into production systems, the initial MVP implementation often reduces to a naive pattern: parse the incoming JSON payload and trigger downstream workers. However, during security audits, threat modeling, and penetration testing, this naive ingestion pipeline reveals critical architectural vulnerabilities: Payload Tampering & Signature Bypass : If the raw payload is modified in transit or generated by an unauthorized party, the server processes forged data without detection. articles.title: Bigger AI models aren't always better: how a 70B model beat a 280B one by reading more
articles.excerpt: For a few years, the way to build a better AI model was simple. Make it bigger. Then in 2022 DeepMind trained a model called Chinchilla. It had 70 billion parameters. It beat their own older model, Go…
articles.body: For a few years, the way to build a better AI model was simple. Make it bigger. Then in 2022 DeepMind trained a model called Chinchilla. It had 70 billion parameters. It beat their own older model, Gopher, which had 280 billion . A quarter of the size, better scores. How? Chinchilla didn't have a smarter design. It just read a lot more. I wanted to see that for myself, so I trained a pile of tiny models on my laptop. Here's what happened. First, two words Parameters : the adjustable numbers inside a model. "70B" means 70 billion of them. Think of it as the size of the model's brain. Tokens : the chunks of text a model reads while training. Think of it as how much it studied. Training costs compute, and compute is roughly parameters times tokens .

articles.title: How upload_tracker.py Keeps a Re-Run From Double-Posting Your Stock Batch
articles.excerpt: I ran the same batch twice. Not on purpose, obviously. The upload script hit a network timeout halfway through pushing 40 files to Adobe Stock, I fixed what I thought was the issue, and re-ran the who…
articles.body: I ran the same batch twice. Not on purpose, obviously. The upload script hit a network timeout halfway through pushing 40 files to Adobe Stock, I fixed what I thought was the issue, and re-ran the whole thing. Twenty-three files went up twice. Adobe's duplicate detection caught most of them, but the review queue took longer, and getting duplicates pulled is the kind of account noise you do not want when you are trying to build a clean submission history on three platforms at once. That night I wrote upload_tracker.py . It is the least glamorous script in my pipeline and the one I would keep if I could only keep two. Here is what it does and why the problem it solves is worse than it looks.
articles.author: Muhamad Revanza Rafif Hamdani

articles.title: The Simple Ledger That Stops Double-Posting on Adobe, Vecteezy and Dreamstime
articles.excerpt: Last March I ran my upload batch twice. The first run hung halfway through on a flaky connection, so I did what anyone does: I ran it again. Adobe accepted the duplicates without complaint. Vecteezy d…
articles.body: Last March I ran my upload batch twice. The first run hung halfway through on a flaky connection, so I did what anyone does: I ran it again. Adobe accepted the duplicates without complaint. Vecteezy did not. I spent a Sunday afternoon deleting 60-some submissions one by one, and I got a warning email explaining that resubmitting identical content violates their contributor terms. That was the moment I stopped trusting memory and wrote a ledger. This post is about the boring fix: a plain-text ledger and strict CSV headers. It is not exciting, but it is the difference between a pipeline you trust and one you babysit. The CSV header is a gate, not a suggestion All three stock platforms parse your upload CSV before anything else, and a wrong header means instant rejection. Not a warning.
articles.author: Muhamad Revanza Rafif Hamdani

articles.title: Shopify authorizationCode to paymentId: The Silent Reconciliation Trap
articles.excerpt: Shopify deprecated the authorizationCode field on OrderTransaction in the Admin GraphQL API, starting with the 2026-01 version, and recommends you switch to paymentId. The migration guidance is a one…
articles.body: Shopify deprecated the authorizationCode field on OrderTransaction in the Admin GraphQL API, starting with the 2026-01 version, and recommends you switch to paymentId . The migration guidance is a one line find and replace: swap authorizationCode for paymentId in your queries. It compiles, it runs, the API returns a 200 , and your payment reconciliation is now quietly wrong. This is a sharper trap than a field simply going away, because the two fields are not the same kind of value. Here is the sentence from Shopify's own deprecation notice that matters most: paymentId returns a Shopify-specific identifier, which differs from the provider-specific value in authorizationCode . A plain rename assumes the new field is the old field under a new name. It is not.
articles.author: DriftSignal

articles.title: OVHcloud CLI Release Hijack: Verify Downloads, Lock Releases
articles.excerpt: If you installed or updated the OVHcloud CLI (ovhcloud) between 12:47 and 14:21 UTC on 19 October 2026 and ended up on v0.11.0 through v0.15.0, treat every secret readable from that machine as stolen.…
articles.body: If you installed or updated the OVHcloud CLI (ovhcloud) between 12:47 and 14:21 UTC on 19 October 2026 and ended up on v0.11.0 through v0.15.0, treat every secret readable from that machine as stolen. An attacker used a hijacked developer account to replace the release archives, and OVHcloud's own advisory says the build was meant to harvest secrets from disk[1]. The fix for maintainers is one checkbox: GitHub immutable releases lock a published release's assets and tag[7]. Below: who is affected, what to do tonight, why mutable release assets made this possible, a table of defences, how to switch immutability on, and how to verify a CLI before you run it. TL;DR Affected: ovhcloud-cli v0.11.0 to v0.15.0 downloaded 12:47 to 14:21 UTC on 19 Oct 2026 (macOS, Linux, Windows x86_64 archives).

articles.excerpt: If Blue Origin goes public, it will have to meet the expectations of shareholders. Jeff Bezos may therefore want to establish a stronger business before committing to a listing.
articles.body: Daniel Biedermann is a partner at NewSpace Capital. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . Jeff Bezos , the founder and former CEO of Amazon, recently said that Blue Origin , his space technology company, is likely to go public in the coming years. The announcement has (unsurprisingly) attracted considerable attention, not least because Bezos has spent more than two decades financing the company largely from his personal wealth. He has invested billions of dollars in developing rockets , spacecraft and other forms of technology, often with very little prospect of an immediate return. But although Bezos has now raised the possibility of an initial public offering, he has given no firm indication of when one might happen.

articles.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
articles.excerpt: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tec…
articles.body: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.

articles.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
articles.excerpt: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massi…
articles.body: _____________ THE PLACE Pyeongtaek, South Korea Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex.
